title: Hospices the federal scoring system ranks as outliers
question: Which Bay Area hospices does the federal government's own screening index place furthest from their peers, what drives the score, and what has Medicare paid them?
finding: 111 Bay Area hospices were scored for fiscal 2025. Their middle score is 5 of 16, against 6 for California and 6 nationally; 4 scored 10 or more, where the top tenth of the country begins (16% of California hospices do). The highest is Careplus Hospice Services, Inc, Livermore, at 12 (no continuous-care or inpatient days all year; few visits in the last two days of life; many stays of 180 days or more; many patients discharged alive); Medicare paid it $2.7 million in fiscal 2024. 8 scored 4 or more of 8 on the care-pattern half of the index, and for 4 Medicare paid other providers at least five times the California middle figure ($7.86) per hospice day. 4 of the 13 highest-scoring hospices are also in the existing new-or-fast-growing screen.
how: The federal index (the Service and Spending Variation Index) is the sum of two halves, each 0 to 8. One half ranks the total Medicare paid to other providers for a hospice's patients while they were on hospice. The other gives one point for each of eight care patterns, listed in the column "What scored a point". The agency says the purpose is "to identify hospices that may be outliers compared to their peers." Scores are the California rows of the federal workbook for fiscal 2025 (October 2024 to September 2025); Bay Area means the hospice's federal number is in the Bay Area agency table. Medicare payments are from the federal post-acute file for fiscal 2024, the latest year published. Owners with 5% or more come from the federal enrollment record. The last column checks the same cuts used by the existing hospice, owner and address screens.
limits: The index is a screening tool; a high score is a reason to look and proves nothing. The spending half ranks total dollars, not dollars per patient, so every large hospice scores high on it: the long-established nonprofit and chain hospices near the top are there for size. The care-pattern half is the better guide, and each pattern has ordinary causes: a hospice serving nursing-home residents or patients with dementia has longer stays and more patients who leave alive; a small hospice can have no inpatient days in a year; and six of the eight thresholds are set at the 25th or 75th percentile of all hospices, so about a quarter of them score on each of those. Very small hospices have withheld figures (shown blank). A hospice licensed since 2020 is new. Owners are as recorded for the linked agency and can be out of date.
